items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] ‘I’m not ready to go to jail’: co-founder of Egypt’s last independent media outlet faces prison
items.content_html:
Mada Masr, the news site co-founded by Lina Attalah just before the 2013 military coup, is fighting for its life after being shut down, but its journalists have not given up hope

Facing a year in prison for running Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr, Lina Attalah is trying to focus on the everyday: waking at dawn to hear the birds sing before Cairo’s streets come alive and visiting Mada Masr’s shuttered offices with her reporters to water the plants and feed their four cats.

Attalah is the reluctant face of Egypt’s embattled independent press at a moment of crisis. In the last six weeks, Egyptian authorities have waged a renewed crackdown on the few remaining independent media outlets left in the country, beginning with the arrest of the entire newsroom of the factchecking website Matsadaash.

Paz Rodríguez woke up about 5am at her home in Milpa Alta, a suburb of Mexico City, on 20 March 2021. She thought about her plans for the day: pick up yellow lilies and cacti from her mother’s house and sell them in the market. Later that evening, they would cook mole, a traditional Mexican dish, together.

She reached for her phone, which was flooded with texts from her sister, Oliviera Rodríguez. “Mum’s dog is barking a lot,” she had written. “I keep calling and she won’t respond.”

items.title: [euronews.com] Five EU states plan Rwanda hub for rejected asylum seekers
items.content_html: Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to announce a plan in Vienna to transfer some migrants whose asylum claims have been rejected after final review to a return hub in Rwanda, the first such EU facility outside the bloc. The governments say the scheme would comply with EU and international law. The pilot is expected to cover about 100 to 200 people, with the first transfers planned for 2027. The countries argue that sending people to a third country when their country of origin will not take them back could increase removals and deter irregular migration. The proposed facilities would be open, but migrants could remain in Rwanda indefinitely if they cannot be returned to their home countries. Rights groups and legal experts warn that the plan could expose migrants to abuse and leave them without clear ways to challenge decisions. The 2023 UK Supreme Court ruling against a similar Rwanda arrangement provides a legal precedent. The five states are expected to work out detailed terms in early 2027 before launching the pilot later that year.

items.title: [news.err.ee] Estonia announces closure of three Russia crossings used by pedestrians and freight
items.content_html: Estonia plans to close its three remaining road crossings with Russia on Dec. 1, ending pedestrian and freight traffic at Narva, Luhamaa and Koidula. The crossings are among the few land links still operating between Russia and the European Union since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Moscow suspended vehicle traffic at Narva in February 2024, but pedestrians continued to cross. The decision follows an attempted arson and explosion at Threod Systems, an Estonian maker of reconnaissance and attack drones in Viimsi, near Tallinn. Estonia says Russia’s military intelligence service, the GRU, ordered the attack. Eight residents of Latvia were detained; authorities said company security stopped the attempt before it caused significant damage or injuries. How long the closure will last remains undecided. Interior Minister Igor Taro said Estonian ministers would decide whether it is temporary or indefinite. People from Estonia who are in Russia, along with truck drivers, have been given about two weeks to return before crossing becomes more difficult. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna was also due to raise possible new sanctions at an EU foreign ministers’ meeting in Brussels on Monday, Nov. 16.

items.title: [channelnewsasia.com] ASEAN keeps Myanmar leaders barred, ties return to peace-plan progress
items.content_html: Southeast Asian leaders agreed on Nov. 15 to maintain restrictions on Myanmar’s political leaders’ participation in Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) summits and foreign ministers’ meetings, and set conditions for their return. A career diplomat from Myanmar’s foreign ministry represented the country at the Manila summit, rather than its military-backed president or foreign minister. The leaders said restoring full political representation would depend on “sustained and concrete progress” on ASEAN’s Five-Point Consensus, the bloc’s plan to end violence and advance dialogue, mediation and humanitarian aid. They called on the military, security forces and armed groups to stop attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and pressed for a nationwide ceasefire and safe aid access. The leaders acknowledged that implementation remains insufficient; Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Theresa Lazaro cited ongoing bombings and displacement. The statement also encouraged ASEAN members to engage Myanmar individually, in consultation with the bloc’s chair, while keeping the consensus as the main framework. Leaders did not decide in Manila when Myanmar could return to high-level political meetings; the question is expected to pass to Singapore when it assumes ASEAN’s rotating chair in 2027.

items.title: [usnews.com] Trump, Xi and Putin set first trilateral talks on nuclear arms
items.content_html: The White House said Friday, Nov. 13, that President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin plan to meet Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It would be the three leaders’ first joint meeting. Trump intends to raise nuclear arms reductions and the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran; a senior U.S. official said Ukraine would not be on the agenda and no agreement was expected. The meeting follows the February expiration of New START, the last nuclear arms pact between Washington and Moscow, which left the two countries’ arsenals without limits for the first time in more than five decades. Trump rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty for a year and has called for a new agreement that includes China. Beijing has resisted trilateral arms talks, arguing that the United States and Russia hold much larger nuclear stockpiles. Trump is scheduled to meet Xi separately before the three-way session but has no one-on-one meeting planned with Putin. A senior U.S. official said Washington is handling Ukraine through a separate channel with Kyiv and Moscow. Trump leaves for Asia on Monday, Nov. 16, with stops in the Philippines and Shenzhen.

items.title: [elpais.com] US designates three Guatemalan drug-trafficking networks as terrorists
items.content_html: On November 13, the US government designated Los Lorenzana, Los Huistas, and Los Mendoza, three Guatemalan criminal networks, as terrorist groups because of their ties to Mexican cartels and their role in drug trafficking. The State Department classified Los Lorenzana as a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist; the Treasury Department added Los Huistas and Los Mendoza to the latter category. The measures block assets under US jurisdiction and prohibit, with some exceptions, US persons from transacting with the groups. The designation of Los Lorenzana also makes it possible to prosecute anyone who knowingly provides them with material support. The sanctions may affect foreign banks that facilitate significant transactions. Washington links Los Mendoza to the Sinaloa Cartel and Los Huistas to Sinaloa and the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG). The designation of Los Lorenzana will take effect after its publication in the Federal Register. The US embassy clarified that the measures do not, by themselves, authorize military operations in Guatemala.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] German parliament gives spy agencies powers to hack, sabotage and enter homes
items.content_html: Germany’s Bundestag voted on Nov. 13 to give the foreign intelligence service BND and domestic intelligence agency BfV new powers to disrupt threats, including cyber operations and, under certain conditions, covert entry into homes and business premises. The measure passed 309-190, with 71 abstentions. The government says it responds to foreign espionage and sabotage, including activity it attributes to Russia. The BND will be able to conduct covert operations abroad, while the BfV may take action against property and computer systems when it identifies specific threats. The agencies also gain expanded digital surveillance tools, including access to encrypted communications and AI-assisted data analysis. Arrests and overt searches remain police responsibilities, and an independent oversight body will review certain intrusive measures in advance. The government says the reform equips Germany to counter hybrid attacks; critics warn it weakens the postwar boundary between intelligence gathering and police powers. Modernizing the agencies under the bill will take years, and the Financial Times reported that recruitment in key areas is already proving difficult.

items.content_html: World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Director Luke J. Lindberg called for an end to Sudan’s war and more donor funding after visiting Goz Al-Salam camp for displaced people. About 34 million people—nearly two-thirds of Sudan’s population—need humanitarian assistance, the United Nations says. The war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces began in April 2023. Funding cuts have reduced WFP food assistance from more than 4 million people in August to just over 3 million, leaving an estimated 900,000 without support. WFP is seeking $520 million to assist 5.4 million people through April 2027, while insecurity, blocked roads and flood damage are also hindering deliveries.

items.title: [theguardian.com] UK and EU seek Brexit reset deal before November 20 summit
items.content_html: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said a “win-win” agreement with the European Union could be reached before a summit in Brussels on November 20, where the sides aim to conclude deals on food trade, carbon emissions and youth mobility. He said the agreements could lower costs for consumers and businesses and resemble what voters expected when they backed Brexit in 2016. Draft texts would reduce post-Brexit checks on food and farm exports, link the UK and EU emissions-trading systems, and create a youth travel, study and work scheme. One draft described in reporting would allow stays of up to three years. The European Union has tied implementation of the food and emissions agreements to a deal on lower university tuition fees for European students in Britain, a demand Burnham has not publicly accepted. London is also pressing for British firms to qualify for the EU’s planned “Made in Europe” industrial policy, while the EU wants safeguards against Chinese electric vehicles entering its market through Britain. Burnham said negotiations could continue until the last moment. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa are due to meet him at the summit.

items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. floods force evacuations, shelter orders as roads close
items.content_html:
🎨 🌾 🏔️ 🔭 ✏️

Heavy rain and flooding across British Columbia’s South Coast prompted shelter-in-place advisories near Squamish and in Pemberton Valley, while evacuation orders covered parts of Pemberton and Lil’wat Nation on Thursday, Nov. 12. Some areas received more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours, and floodwater closed Highway 99 east of Pemberton and roads near Squamish. The entire Village of Pemberton was under an evacuation alert. Evacuation orders also remained in effect in Zeballos, where flooding and landslide risks threatened about 30 properties. The release of water from the Cheakamus Dam flooded roads near Squamish and was intended to make room in the reservoir for more rain. Officials expected river levels to crest Thursday and then recede. Rain eased in some areas, but Vancouver Island remained under rainfall and flood warnings, and forecasters were tracking more storm systems expected over the weekend.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Rats, dengue and an all-day stench: can Panama City solve its waste crisis?
items.content_html:
For decades, mountains of waste have blighted poor neighbourhoods on the edge of the city. But as the problems spread, a belated reckoning is under way

Life in San Miguelito has long been dictated by rubbish. Routes to the shop are carefully navigated to avoid pungent mountains of rotting waste, some visible from space. Driving during the rainy season is a perilous obstacle course, dodging black bin bags and rusty fridges in the middle of the road. Children are taught early to avoid the river, the rubbish, the rats, yet mosquito-borne diseases still stalk the community.

For Yamileth, who lives with her family on one of the steep, narrow streets that thread the hillside neighbourhood, the waste is a constant backdrop to daily life. Mornings are punctuated by the stench and buzz of flies, and in the evenings you can hear rats scuttling and stray dogs rustling as they rip open bags in search of food among the rubbish heaps, known in slang as patacones (also the name of a staple side dish made from green plantains).

items.title: [ScienceDaily] Earth's fiery birth may have created hundreds of oceans' worth of water
items.content_html:
🌲 🔭 ✏️

Earth's water may have been born in the planet's fiery atmosphere rather than delivered by icy comets or asteroids. Scientists discovered that rocky pebbles reacting with hydrogen under extreme heat can produce water in minutes, potentially generating hundreds of oceans' worth during Earth's formation. The findings suggest that water may be a natural part of how rocky planets form, rather than something that must arrive from space.
